A $TSM Spokesperson has reportedly denied exploring 3D DRAM per Tom's Hardware. 

After a report yesterday from The Information stated TSMC's production plans were from $NVDA's request. 

The implications would have put TSMC in competition with $MU, SK Hynix, and Samsung and set off narratives about TSm disrupting the biggest memory makers. 

There's something frustrating with there's market moving headlines both ways. It just creates more confusion and volatility... 

Especially if something (like $NVDA CEO honeypot allegations) or the TSM report yesterday turns out untrue.
@aleabitoreddit Do you really think Jensen & that spy are banging each other? And how does it affect AI trade ?

If someone asked me 10 years ago what I'd be doing in the future,

Answering questions on Jensen + Spys banging each other and implications on the AI trade would not be in mind

My response to that question is: how am i supposed to know? 

On AI trade implications: $NVDA probably wanted to sell more chips anyway (to China) for revenue and it's extremely unlikely this person had any effect on trade policies. 

The relationship might not even be true... anyway I'll wait until more news comes out.

Yep! That's a fair example with onsemi. But I'm not quite sure it's appropriate to extrapolate from historical examples of mutually agreed contract changes.

And apply that to today's memory market and assume $MU would make concessions if demand/pricing ever drops.  

Micron really went out of their way to emphasize that their SCAs are different relative to historical ones in terms of contractual price floors + binding commitment clauses.

This can be a golden age of investigative journalism. Analyzing filings, records and public data to go deep into a company or government or whatever used to be something that took a team of journalists a long time, so was relatively rare. Now LLMs can 10x investigative research.

AI could do 1000x more research but the jagged frontier currently runs through the fact that the taste for what is an interesting story almost certainly remains human (because the same bottlene is happening in academic research). At least for now.

I think there is way too much concern expressed about verification of AI output in everyday work due to a risk of factual errors.

It used to be true, but data on more recent models suggest they beat human experts, including PhD specialists, in finding facts and checking claims.

Now there might be things to verify beyond errors - points of view, opinions, approaches, etc. But the idea that the job of humans should be checking AI work for mistakes is likely not true today, and good riddance.
AIs may still underperform humans in error rates in some cases, of course, but we need to update our assumptions about how often that occurs.
